Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 77, verse 1–32:

Meccan. It contains eight hundred and sixteen letters, one hundred and eighty-one words, and fifty verses.

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Faqih informed me, saying: Muhammad ibn Zayd al-Adl related to us, saying: Abu Yahya al-Bazzaz related to us, saying: Mansur related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Imran related to us, saying: My father related to us from Mukhallad, from Ali ibn Zayd, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah of al-Mursalat, it is written for him that he is not among the polytheists" [82] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/227.]].

Al-Aswad ibn Yazid narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: I recited "Wa al-Mursalati 'urfan" to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of the jinn while we were travelling [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 19/153.]].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in gusts﴾: meaning the winds, one following another like the mane of a horse (ʿurf al-faras). It was also said: in abundance. The Arabs say: "The people came to so-and-so in one mane (ʿurf wahid)" when they converge upon him in large numbers. This is the meaning reported by Mujahid and Qatadah, and the narration of Abu al-'Ubayd from Ibn Mas'ud, and al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Salih and Muqatil said: it means the angels who are sent with what is known (al-ma'ruf), a single category of God's command and prohibition; this is the narration of Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿And by those that blow violently﴾: meaning the very strong winds.

﴿And by those that scatter widely﴾: meaning the gentle winds. Abu Salih said: they are the clouds (al-mutriq). al-Hasan said: they are the winds that God sends as heralds before His mercy. God swore by the winds three times. Muqatil said: they are the angels who spread out the books.

﴿And by those that separate, separating﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it means the angels who separate truth from falsehood. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: it means the verses of the Qur'an, which separated the lawful from the unlawful. It was also said: it means the rain-bearing clouds, likened to a pregnant she-camel that is distressed when giving birth (al-naqah al-fariq), and she-camels in distress (nuq firaq).

﴿And by those that deliver a reminder﴾: meaning the angels that bring down revelation, akin to His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend﴾ [[Surat al-Qadr: 4.]]. ﴿As an excuse or a warning﴾: meaning excuses (a'dhar) and warnings (indhar). The reciters differed over them. al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read them with lightened pronunciation, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, saying: since they stand in the position of verbal nouns (masdar), meaning "the excusing and the warning," and are not plurals that would be made heavy. al-Hasan read them with heavy pronunciation; this is the narration of al-A'sha and al-Ju'fi from Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and al-Walid from the people of Syria, and Rawh from Ya'qub. (Al-Yaqut: with heavy "nudhr" and light "udhr".) Both are dialectal variants. Ibrahim al-Taymi and Qatadah read "'udhran aw nudhran" with the conjunctive waw and without an alif between them.

﴿What you are promised will surely come to pass. So when the stars are obliterated﴾: their light is effaced. ﴿And when the sky is split open﴾: it is torn apart. ﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾: they are uprooted from their places. ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾: they are assembled for a fixed appointed day. The reciters differed over this word. Abu 'Amr read "wuqqitat" with a waw and a doubled qaf, following the original form; Abu Ja'far read it with a waw and light pronunciation; 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi read "uqitat" with an alif and light qaf; the rest read it with an alif and doubled qaf, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. The Arabs interchange the waw and the hamzah, as in their saying: wakkadtu, akkartu; warrakhtu al-kitab and arrakhtuhu; wuddisha min al-qawm and arrisha; washah and ashah; ukaf and wukaf; wisadah and asadah. al-Nakha'i said: it means "ra'adat" (trembled).

﴿For what day were they deferred?﴾: that is, they were appointed a term (waqqat) from the word ajal. It was also said: they were postponed ﴿for the Day of Decision﴾. ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ ﴿Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾: the deniers among the nations of ancient times. ﴿Then We follow them with the later ones﴾: those who follow their path in disbelief and denial. al-A'raj read "nutbi'hum" with the jussive, and Ibn Mas'ud read "sanutbi'uhum."

﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals. Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Did We not create you from a worthless fluid?﴾ ﴿Then We placed it in a secure place﴾ ﴿for a known term﴾: which is the time of birth. ﴿Then We determined﴾: Ali, al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Talhah, Qatadah, Abu Ishaq, the people of Madinah and Ayyub read it with doubling, from taqdir (determining). This is the choice of al-Kisa'i. The rest read it with lightened pronunciation, from qudrah (power), and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, due to His saying: ﴿So how excellent are the Determiners?﴾ It is possible that the doubled and light readings have the same meaning, as in His saying: ﴿We have determined death among you﴾ [[Surat al-Waqi'ah: 60.]], which is read both ways. ﴿Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Did We not make the earth a receptacle﴾: a container ﴿for the living and the dead﴾: it gathers them alive upon its back, and when they die it gathers them into its belly. [Banan al-Saffar] said: We went out to a graveyard with al-Sha'bi, and he looked at the graveyard and said: "These are the dead." Then he looked at the houses and said: "These are the receptacles of the living."

The root of "kaft" is gathering and drawing together. They used to call the cemetery of Baqi' al-Gharqad a "kafatah," because it is a graveyard that gathers the dead. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Cover your vessels, tie the mouths of your waterskins, close the doors, extinguish the lamps, and restrain your children, for the Devil has a dispersal and a snatching (at night)" [83] [[al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith: 1/342.]], meaning at night. The earth is also called "kafatah."

﴿And We placed in it firm mountains, high, and gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ ﴿Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ Then He informs that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Proceed to a shade of three branches﴾: meaning the smoke of Hell when it rises in three branches. It was also said: it is a neck that comes out of the Fire and divides into three branches. As for the light, it stands over the heads of the believers, the smoke stands over the heads of the hypocrites, and the pure flame stands over the heads of the disbelievers. Muqatil said: it is the pavilion, and the shade is from black smoke. ﴿Neither shady nor protective against the flame.﴾ ﴿It throws up sparks like a fortress﴾: Hell throws sparks, which are what flies off from the fire when it blazes, singular "shararah." ("Sharar" is read by 'Isa, a dialect of Tamim.) The singular is "shararah."

"Ka'l-qasr" (like a fortress): the common readers read the sad with sukun. Ibn Mas'ud said: it means fortresses and cities, and it is the singular of "qasr." This is the narration of al-Wali from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "like a great fortress." al-Qurazi said: upon Hell is a wall, and whatever comes out from behind the wall that returns to it is like a great fortress in size and in the colour of the fire.

Sa'id narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abis, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about His saying: ﴿It throws up sparks like a fortress﴾. He said: "They are large cut pieces of wood. We used to cut wood into pieces of three cubits or more, and less, and store them for winter, and we called them 'qasr'." Mujahid said: they are bundles of trees. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: they are the roots of palm trees and large trees, singular "qasrah," like "tamrah" and "tamr," and "jamrah" and "jamr."

Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas read "kal-qasar" with a fatha on the sad, meaning the necks of palm trees. "Al-qasrah" means the neck, and its plural is "qasr" and "qasarat." Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "kal-qisar" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Abu Hatim said: it is perhaps a dialect, and its parallel in speech is "hajah" and "hawj," as if he returned the pronoun to the wording.

﴿What you are promised will surely come to pass. Meccan. It contains eight hundred and sixteen letters, one hundred and eighty-one words, and fifty verses.

Al-Aswad ibn Yazid narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: I recited "Wa al-Mursalati 'urfan" to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of the jinn while we were travelling [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 19/153.]].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in gusts﴾: meaning the winds, one following another like the mane of a horse (ʿurf al-faras). It was also said: in abundance. ﴿And by those that blow violently﴾: meaning the very strong winds.

Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: it means the verses of the Qur'an, which separated the lawful from the unlawful. It was also said: it means the rain-bearing clouds, likened to a pregnant she-camel that is distressed when giving birth (al-naqah al-fariq), and she-camels in distress (nuq firaq).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: it means the verses of the Qur'an, which separated the lawful from the unlawful. ﴿What you are promised will surely come to pass. So when the stars are obliterated﴾: their light is effaced. ﴿And when the sky is split open﴾: it is torn apart. ﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾: they are uprooted from their places. ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾: they are assembled for a fixed appointed day. The reciters differed over this word. Abu 'Amr read "wuqqitat" with a waw and a doubled qaf, following the original form; Abu Ja'far read it with a waw and light pronunciation; 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi read "uqitat" with an alif and light qaf; the rest read it with an alif and doubled qaf, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. The Arabs interchange the waw and the hamzah, as in their saying: wakkadtu, akkartu; warrakhtu al-kitab and arrakhtuhu; wuddisha min al-qawm and arrisha; washah and ashah; ukaf and wukaf; wisadah and asadah. al-Nakha'i said: it means "ra'adat" (trembled).

﴿For what day were they deferred?﴾: that is, they were appointed a term (waqqat) from the word ajal. It was also said: they were postponed ﴿for the Day of Decision﴾. ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ ﴿Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾: the deniers among the nations of ancient times. ﴿Then We follow them with the later ones﴾: those who follow their path in disbelief and denial. al-A'raj read "nutbi'hum" with the jussive, and Ibn Mas'ud read "sanutbi'uhum."

﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals. Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Did We not create you from a worthless fluid?﴾ ﴿Then We placed it in a secure place﴾ ﴿for a known term﴾: which is the time of birth. ﴿Then We determined﴾: Ali, al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Talhah, Qatadah, Abu Ishaq, the people of Madinah and Ayyub read it with doubling, from taqdir (determining). This is the choice of al-Kisa'i. The rest read it with lightened pronunciation, from qudrah (power), and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, due to His saying: ﴿So how excellent are the Determiners?﴾ It is possible that the doubled and light readings have the same meaning, as in His saying: ﴿We have determined death among you﴾ [[Surat al-Waqi'ah: 60.]], which is read both ways. ﴿Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Did We not make the earth a receptacle﴾: a container ﴿for the living and the dead﴾: it gathers them alive upon its back, and when they die it gathers them into its belly. [Banan al-Saffar] said: We went out to a graveyard with al-Sha'bi, and he looked at the graveyard and said: "These are the dead." Then he looked at the houses and said: "These are the receptacles of the living."

﴿And We placed in it firm mountains, high, and gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ ﴿Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ Then He informs that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Proceed to a shade of three branches﴾: meaning the smoke of Hell when it rises in three branches. It was also said: it is a neck that comes out of the Fire and divides into three branches. As for the light, it stands over the heads of the believers, the smoke stands over the heads of the hypocrites, and the pure flame stands over the heads of the disbelievers. Muqatil said: it is the pavilion, and the shade is from black smoke. ﴿Neither shady nor protective against the flame.﴾ ﴿It throws up sparks like a fortress﴾: Hell throws sparks, which are what flies off from the fire when it blazes, singular "shararah." ("Sharar" is read by 'Isa, a dialect of Tamim.) The singular is "shararah."

Sa'id narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abis, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about His saying: ﴿It throws up sparks like a fortress﴾. He said: "They are large cut pieces of wood. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "kal-qisar" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Abu Hatim said: it is perhaps a dialect, and its parallel in speech is "hajah" and "hawj," as if he returned the pronoun to the wording.

﴿And We placed in it firm mountains, high, and gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ ﴿Woe, that day, to the deniers!﴾ Then He informs that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Proceed to a shade of three branches﴾: meaning the smoke of Hell when it rises in three branches. It was also said: it is a neck that comes out of the Fire and divides into three branches. As for the light, it stands over the heads of the believers, the smoke stands over the heads of the hypocrites, and the pure flame stands over the heads of the disbelievers. Muqatil said: it is the pavilion, and the shade is from black smoke. ﴿Neither shady nor protective against the flame.﴾ ﴿It throws up sparks like a fortress﴾: Hell throws sparks, which are what flies off from the fire when it blazes, singular "shararah." ("Sharar" is read by 'Isa, a dialect of Tamim.) The singular is "shararah."

"Ka'l-qasr" (like a fortress): the common readers read the sad with sukun. Ibn Mas'ud said: it means fortresses and cities, and it is the singular of "qasr." This is the narration of al-Wali from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "like a great fortress." al-Qurazi said: upon Hell is a wall, and whatever comes out from behind the wall that returns to it is like a great fortress in size and in the colour of the fire.

Sa'id narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abis, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about His saying: ﴿It throws up sparks like a fortress﴾. He said: "They are large cut pieces of wood. We used to cut wood into pieces of three cubits or more, and less, and store them for winter, and we called them 'qasr'." Mujahid said: they are bundles of trees. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: they are the roots of palm trees and large trees, singular "qasrah," like "tamrah" and "tamr," and "jamrah" and "jamr."

Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas read "kal-qasar" with a fatha on the sad, meaning the necks of palm trees. "Al-qasrah" means the neck, and its plural is "qasr" and "qasarat." Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "kal-qisar" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Abu Hatim said: it is perhaps a dialect, and its parallel in speech is "hajah" and "hawj," as if he returned the pronoun to the wording.

The rest read *jimalat* with an *alif* and a *kasrah* on the *jim*, as the plural of *jimal* (ropes).
